c.v: We spent this stage proving the machine before writing any robot code. Ubuntu 24.04 runs ROS 2 Jazzy, and a C++ talker and a Python listener exchange messages across two fresh terminals, which proves the middleware works across languages, a stronger claim than one process talking to itself. Gazebo Harmonic runs both headless, for a thousand simulated steps with no window, and with its GUI, publishing the clock and stats topics a later simulation will depend on. The compiler, debugger and sanitizers work too: AddressSanitizer named the exact line of a planted heap overflow before anything real had a chance to hide one.
The decision worth defending is writing every version down before any of this gets used, in
environment.md

, not in memory. A bug three months from now has to be told apart from a bug in a fresh install, and a mismatched compiler or ROS release still passes a naive smoke test until something else depends on the difference.

What we can now show: a listener that heard a talker, a Gazebo world that ran and rendered, and a sanitizer report that named the exact allocation and the exact overflow, with every version behind them written down.

subs.title: Install and verify ROS 2, Gazebo and the compilers

c.v: By the end of this session, ROS 2 Jazzy is installed on Ubuntu 24.04, and a talker and a listener exchange messages in two fresh terminals.

Jazzy is the ROS 2 long-term support release for Ubuntu 24.04 (Noble), supported until 2029. The Test Bench uses it throughout. On Windows, use WSL2 with Ubuntu 24.04. On Windows 11, WSLg shows Linux windows such as RViz and the Gazebo GUI without extra setup.

items.v: Check the Ubuntu version. It must say 24.04. Then bring the system up to date: ROS packages are built against a current Ubuntu.

blocks.text:
lsb_release -ds
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

items.v: Make sure the locale is UTF-8. This is the official sequence:

blocks.text:
locale                                  # look for UTF-8
sudo apt update && sudo apt install locales
sudo locale-gen en_US en_US.UTF-8
sudo update-locale LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 LANG=en_US.UTF-8
export LANG=en_US.UTF-8

items.v: Enable the Universe repository and add the ROS 2 apt source. Since 2025 this is done by installing the
package, which also keeps the signing key current:

blocks.text:
sudo apt install software-properties-common
sudo add-apt-repository universe
sudo apt update && sudo apt install curl -y
export ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/latest | grep -F "tag_name" | awk -F'"' '{print $4}')
curl -L -o /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb "https://github.com/ros-infrastructure/ros-apt-source/releases/download/${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}/ros2-apt-source_${ROS_APT_SOURCE_VERSION}.$(. /etc/os-release && echo ${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-${VERSION_CODENAME}})_all.deb"
sudo dpkg -i /tmp/ros2-apt-source.deb

items.v: Install the development tools (colcon, rosdep and vcstool) and the desktop variant, which includes RViz and the demos:

blocks.text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install ros-dev-tools
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop

items.v: Source ROS in every new terminal, and set up rosdep once:

blocks.text:
echo "source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash" >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
sudo rosdep init
rosdep update

items.v: Verify the install in two terminals you open now, so you also know

blocks.text:
ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker     # terminal 1: prints "Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'" ...
ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener    # terminal 2: prints "I heard: [Hello World: 1]" ...

c.v: Stop both with Ctrl+C. The C++ and Python demos talking to each other also proves the middleware works across languages.
You are done when the listener hears the talker in two fresh terminals. If a command fails, write down the exact error and what fixed it. That note is the start of your debugging record.
The commands above follow the official guide as of September 2026. If a step fails, check the
ROS 2 Jazzy installation guide
for changes.
By the end of this session, Gazebo runs both headless and with its GUI, and the C++ compiler, the debugger and the sanitizers work.

items.v: Install Gazebo through ROS. For Jazzy, the recommended version is Gazebo Harmonic, and
installs it together with the ROS bridge:

blocks.text:
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros-gz
gz sim --version

items.v: Run an empty world without the GUI for 1000 steps. It should exit by itself:
Run it with the GUI, and list its topics from a second terminal:

blocks.text:
gz sim empty.sdf        # terminal 1: a window with an empty world
gz topic -l             # terminal 2: shows /clock, /stats and others

c.v: If the window stays black or the GUI crashes under WSL, try software rendering with
export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1
before
gz sim
, and write down whether it helped.

items.v: Install and check the C++ tools:

blocks.text:
sudo apt install build-essential cmake gdb git
g++ --version | head -1      # 13.x on Ubuntu 24.04
cmake --version | head -1
gdb --version | head -1

c.v: Create
~/bench-notes/environment.md
. It is the proof for this topic, and the first piece of reproducibility: anyone, including you in three months, can rebuild the same setup. It stays outside
~/test_bench
for now, because the Test Bench repository doesn't exist until the skeleton topic, and
git clone
refuses a folder that already has files in it. The skeleton topic moves it into the repository as
docs/environment.md
. Fill it from these commands:

blocks.text:
lsb_release -ds
uname -r
printenv ROS_DISTRO
gz sim --version
g++ --version | head -1
cmake --version | head -1
gdb --version | head -1
dpkg-query -W ros-jazzy-desktop ros-jazzy-ros-gz ros-dev-tools
